title: Fast and accurate rare-event simulation by Markov chain Monte Carlo for general quantum codes
abstract: The splitting method estimates logical error rates of quantum error-correcting codes deep in the rare-event regime, where direct Monte Carlo sampling is prohibitively expensive. It relies on a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampler of faulty configurations, usually driven by one-bit-flip proposals. However, one-bit flips have been reported to be trapped on some codes, which biases the estimate. To address this issue, we propose a new kernel that combines locally balanced one-bit-flip proposals with a cluster-exchange move. We benchmark both kernels and direct Monte Carlo on twelve codes under code-capacity bit-flip noise in two ways, by comparing the mean fault weight with an MCMC-independent reference and by measuring the computation time to reach a fixed accuracy. In the first, our kernel agrees with the reference on every code, including those where one-bit flips are trapped. In the second, it is faster than one-bit flips wherever they are trapped, by orders of magnitude on some codes. Furthermore, at the lowest error rate, it is faster than direct Monte Carlo on every code, by more than four orders of magnitude on some.
summary: This paper introduces an advanced Markov Chain Monte Carlo kernel to accurately and efficiently estimate the logical error rate of quantum error-correcting codes. By combining local proposals with cluster-exchange moves, the method overcomes trapping issues inherent in simpler samplers. The results demonstrate that this new kernel achieves massive speedups over direct simulation methods, enabling reliable analysis at extremely low error rates.
main_problem: The primary goal is to estimate the logical error rate ($P_L$) of quantum error-correcting codes in the rare-event regime, where direct Monte Carlo sampling is computationally infeasible.
main_result: The proposed MCMC kernel, combining locally balanced one-bit-flip proposals with a cluster-exchange move, is shown to be significantly faster and unbiased compared to standard one-bit-flip methods or direct Monte Carlo sampling.
method: The authors employ the splitting method, which estimates $P_L$ as a product of ratios estimated via Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling, utilizing a novel, enhanced proposal kernel.
model_or_system: The study focuses on general quantum error-correcting codes (e.g., surface codes, BB codes) under code-capacity bit-flip or depolarizing noise models.
key_observables: Logical error rate ($P_L$), mean fault weight ($\mathbb{E}_F[w]$), and computation time required to reach a fixed accuracy.
important_parameters: Physical error rates ($p$) ranging from $10^{-1}$ down to $10^{-5}$, and the structure of the quantum codes themselves.
main_assumptions: The success of the method relies on the availability of an MCMC-independent reference value for benchmarking, and the ergodicity of the proposed kernel on general codes remains unproven.
figures_summary: Figures compare the speedup of the proposed kernel against direct Monte Carlo and one-bit-flip kernels, showing exponential speedups at low error rates.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of rare-event estimation, details the limitations of simple MCMC kernels (like one-bit-flips), proposes the combined kernel (Z-obf+ce), and validates its performance through rigorous benchmarking against reference calculations.
why_interesting: The development of efficient simulation techniques for rare events is crucial for assessing the fault-tolerance thresholds of quantum computation, directly impacting the feasibility of large-scale quantum processors.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Speedup of our kernel, Zanella one-bit flips with clus- ter exchange (Z-obf+ce), at p = 10−5 on the twelve codes, the time to accuracy T2% (Sec. IV D) of direct Monte Carlo (squares) or of the one-bit-flip kernel obf (triangles) divided by that of Z-obf+ce, from Tables IV and V. An open marker with a line to the right is a lower bound, where the slower method did not reach the target within its budget. The stan- dard errors defined in Sec. IV D are smaller than the markers. The dashed line marks equal time.

FIG. 2. Time to accuracy T2% of Eq. (44) in core-seconds for Z-obf+ce (circles) and direct Monte Carlo (squares) on the twelve benchmark codes. Each panel corresponds to one physical error rate p and each row to one code. An open square with a line extending to the right marks a lower bound, where direct Monte Carlo did not reach the 2% target within its budget, as in Table IV. Each symbol is the mean over the ten runs of Sec. IV D, and its horizontal error bar gives the bootstrap standard error of that mean over the runs. Most error bars are smaller than the symbols.

FIG. 3. Time to accuracy T2% of Eq. (44) versus pcluster at m = 2 and p = 10−4 on five codes, measured as in Table IV over five runs of 50 chains. Each cell gives T2% divided by the smallest reached value in its row, so the fastest reached setting for each code has the value 1 and darker cells are slower. Parentheses give the standard error of this ratio, propagated from the bootstrap standard errors of the two times. A hatched cell with ≥is a lower bound where at least one run did not reach the target within 2,048,000 steps. The outlined column is the default pcluster = 0.3.
